figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Conceptual differences between Hawkes processes (1) and neural TPPs (2) on an event sequence ($\bullet$ type A, $\blacktriangle$ type B). Top (Hawkes process). Each past event interacts via a kernel response $\phi_{d_{i}\to d}(t-t_{i})$ (colored curves) on top of a (possibly time-varying) baseline $\mu_{d}(t)$ (thin solid line). The total intensity (upper sub-panel) is the sum of baseline and active kernels. At a query time $t$, the intensity thus decomposes into the sum of the baseline and the kernel values. Bottom (Neural TPP). The same event history is consumed by a neural encoder, which produces a hidden state at each event location. The head of the neural TPP projects this encoding to an intensity function. Conceptually, this allows the neural TPP to model higher-order non-additive effects between events, in exchange for losing the interpretable decomposition of the Hawkes process.
figures.headline: Hawkes intensities are additive sums of baseline and kernel terms, whereas neural TPPs allow non-additive effects between events.
citing_sentences: See Figure 1 for a conceptual visualization.
See Shchur et al. (2021) for a survey of neural TPP architectures, and Figure 1 for a conceptual comparison with Hawkes processes.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Flexibility acts on the time density. Change in per-event test log-likelihood (nats) vs. spline knot count $K$ (relative to $K{=}20$), for NeuralSplineTPP (intensity-head knots) and Spline/Spline Hawkes (kernel knots), on three datasets (all datasets in Tables 22 and 19). Left: the continuous time term $\log p(t)$ increases with $K$ on Retweet and Amazon. Middle: scored by the probability of the recorded time bin (Retweet: 1, Amazon: 0.01, MIMIC-IV: 1 min), it increases only on Amazon. Right: the type-conditional term $\log p(d\mid t)$ does not improve with $K$.
figures.headline: Adding spline knots raises the time term on Retweet and Amazon, while the type-conditional term does not improve on any dataset.
citing_sentences: Figure 2 and Table 22 sweep the spline knot count $K$ for NeuralSplineTPP (intensity head) and Spline/Spline Hawkes (kernel): from $K=10$ to $400$, $\log p(t)$ rises on Retweet and Amazon by 0.9–1.6 nats for both models and stays flat on the other datasets, while $\log p(d\mid t)$ does not improve on any dataset.
Scored by the probability of the recorded time bin instead (Appendix I), the gain from more knots vanishes on Retweet but persists on Amazon, whose time stamps lie on no grid (Figure 2).
The knot-count sweep (Table 23, Figure 2) is run separately (20,000 steps on the standard benchmarks, learning rates 0.1 and 0.01 without per-model adjustment).

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Relationships between the key quantities of a multivariate temporal point process. The top row constructs the survival objects from the per-type conditional intensities $\lambda_{d}^{*}(t)$: summation across types yields the ground intensity $\lambda^{*}(t)$, integration over time yields the cumulative intensity $\Lambda^{*}(t_{i-1},t)$, and the survival $S^{*}(\tau)$ and CDF $F^{*}(\tau)$ of the next-event time follow from $\Lambda^{*}$ by $\exp(-\,\cdot\,)$ and $1-\cdot$. The middle row shows how the next-event densities are constructed at merge nodes ($\times$, $/$): each density is formed by combining two top-row quantities, and the resulting expression is the label on the outgoing arrow. In addition, the time marginal is recovered as $p^{*}(t)=\sum_{d}p^{*}(t,d)$, the type marginal as $p^{*}(d)=\int_{t_{i-1}}^{\infty}p^{*}(t,d)\,dt$, and the time conditional as $p^{*}(t\mid d)=p^{*}(t,d)/p^{*}(d)$. Quantities shown in red ($p^{*}(d)$ and $p^{*}(t\mid d)$) are expensive to evaluate when starting from intensities: both require the unbounded integral defining $p^{*}(d)$, which has no closed form except for trivial cases such as the homogeneous Poisson process and otherwise demands numerical quadrature with $\Lambda^{*}$ evaluated at every quadrature point. Stars denote conditioning on the history $\mathcal{H}_{t_{i-1}}$; $\tau=t-t_{i-1}$.
figures.headline: Type marginal and time conditional densities are costly from intensities, since they need unbounded integrals with numerical quadrature.
citing_sentences: Figure 3 summarizes how these objects relate to one another.

abstract: Temporal point processes (TPPs) are the canonical framework for event sequence data, with applications spanning seismology, social media, and electronic health records. Recently, neural TPPs have been reported to substantially outperform classical TPPs, such as Hawkes processes, but these comparisons pitted flexible neural models against Hawkes processes in their most restricted form and did not consider large-scale medical data. Here, we revisit this comparison through a systematic evaluation of Poisson and Hawkes processes of increasing flexibility against neural TPPs, on five established benchmark datasets and on two large-scale medical evaluation tasks derived from UK Biobank disease histories and MIMIC-IV ICU records, under autoregressive next-event prediction. First, the previously reported gap between Hawkes processes and neural TPPs largely disappears once Hawkes processes are equipped with flexible, learnable baselines and kernels. Second, the flexibility of the intensity parametrization also limits prior neural TPPs: a Transformer with a spline-based intensity head outperforms previous intensity-based neural TPPs and is on par with the intensity-free model. Decomposing the log-likelihood into a time term $\log p(t)$ and a type term $\log p(d\mid t)$, we find that this flexibility advantage lies almost entirely in the time density: more flexibility does not improve the type term. On these benchmarks, the gains of neural TPPs thus lie mostly in modeling when events occur, not which. Third, our results underscore the value of complex datasets for evaluating TPPs: only on the MIMIC-IV ICU records do neural TPPs retain an advantage in the type term. Our results inform both future method development and practitioners’ model choice. We release our framework, TorchPP, as an open-source package with consistent implementations of classical and neural TPPs.

sections.body: The paper re-evaluates Poisson and Hawkes processes against neural TPPs under a unified protocol. Hawkes models get learnable baselines and kernels, plus an inhibitive variant. Evaluation covers five standard benchmarks, a 1,257-type UK Biobank disease-history task, and a 117-type MIMIC-IV ICU task. Scope is limited: Cox-type models and flow-, diffusion-, and state-space-based TPPs are excluded. The section also introduces TorchPP, an open-source PyTorch package implementing classical and neural TPPs.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Prior neural-versus-Hawkes comparisons used rigid Hawkes models and omitted medical data, so this paper re-evaluates them.

sections.body: The section defines a multivariate TPP through its conditional intensity and log-likelihood, which sums the log-intensity at observed events and subtracts the integrated intensity. A Hawkes process adds a baseline to a sum of pairwise triggering kernels, and the classical choice is a constant baseline with an exponential kernel. Neural TPPs replace these terms with a history encoder and an output head. Most heads use Softplus, which blocks a closed-form cumulative intensity. Prior benchmarks compared neural TPPs only with rigid exponential-kernel Hawkes processes or self-correcting processes.
sections.heading: Background and Related Work
sections.headline: Hawkes processes sum a baseline and pairwise kernels, while neural TPPs learn intensities from encoded event history.

sections.body: Hawkes variants cross constant or spline baselines with exponential or spline kernels, and add inhibitive versions that use a Softplus clamp with numerical integration. Neural models share a Transformer encoder, except NHP and IntensityFree, and differ mainly in the output head, from a time-constant head to a spline head. Datasets are the five EasyTPP benchmarks, UK Biobank disease histories, and MIMIC-IV ICU stays. Hyperparameters are tuned on validation log-likelihood, and each model is trained with five seeds. Integrated metrics use only the first 1,000 test sequences, or the first 500 on MIMIC-IV.
sections.heading: Evaluation Design
sections.headline: Hawkes models gain spline baselines and kernels, and neural models vary only the output head, all under one likelihood.

sections.body: Table 2 shows that the best Hawkes variant matches or beats the softplus-headed neural TPPs on all five standard datasets in joint log-likelihood. The remaining Taxi gap to the flexible neural models is 0.09 nats. Amazon is the exception, where the flexible neural models retain a clear advantage. On MIMIC-IV, NeuralSplineTPP leads the best Hawkes variant by 0.45 nats in joint log-likelihood and has higher time-conditional accuracy, 38.3% versus 33.5%. A knot sweep raises the time term by 0.9–1.6 nats on Retweet and Amazon but does not improve the type term.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: Flexible Hawkes models narrow most of the gap, and neural gains mainly appear in the time term rather than the type term.

sections.body: The discussion argues that prior Hawkes baselines were benchmarked too narrowly and that the standard datasets rely mainly on first-order temporal structure. Amazon and MIMIC-IV are where neural models keep an advantage. Future benchmarks should use data with long-range or higher-order dependence, such as electronic health records, and should handle discretized times and simultaneous events. Stated limitations include scope, a next-event-only task, seven datasets, an MIMIC-IV subset without device or laboratory markers, UKB covariates not modeled, and knot placement that may favor the neural model at short range.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Standard benchmarks look dominated by pairwise structure, so a flexible Hawkes process is a sensible practical starting point.

sections.body: The conclusion states that the earlier gap between Hawkes processes and neural TPPs came largely from under-specified models. Most datasets show little evidence for substantial interactions beyond pairwise ones, which calls for harder evaluation sets. Flexible baselines and kernels let Hawkes processes stay competitive on some large-scale medical data. For neural TPPs, flexibility of the intensity parametrization was also a limiting factor. The authors release TorchPP as a modular PyTorch framework covering terminating and right-censored sequences under one interface.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The reported gap was largely an artifact of under-specified models, and flexible intensities also limit neural TPPs.

sections.body: Appendix A describes the TorchPP abstraction, cumulative-intensity inversion sampling, termination and right-censoring, and differences from EasyTPP, with a validation table for THP and SAHP. It also reproduces EasyTPP's Hawkes baseline with tick and reports the refitted accuracies. Other appendices give model details, the hyperparameter search, data preparation for the medical tasks, metrics beyond the main tables, non-stationary Hawkes controls on MIMIC-IV, and calibration. The calibration appendix reports time-rescaling distances and expected calibration error for four models with a closed-form cumulative intensity.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers implementation, EasyTPP comparison, Hawkes baseline reproduction, extra metrics, knot sweeps, and calibration.
